design_detail: Multisite randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (COMBINE; clinicaltrials.gov NCT00006206) at 11 US academic sites, January 2001 to January 2004. 1383 recently abstinent adults with DSM-IV alcohol dependence were randomized to 9 groups. Eight groups (n=1226) formed a 2×2×2 factorial design: naltrexone or placebo, acamprosate or placebo, and combined behavioral intervention (CBI, up to 20 sessions with a specialist) or none, all with medical management (MM, 9 sessions with a health care professional focused on adherence and abstinence). A ninth group (n=157) received CBI alone, without pills or MM, to address the effect of taking pills and seeing a health professional; it lies outside the factorial. Treatment lasted 16 weeks, with follow-up to 1 year after treatment (week 68). Coprimary outcomes: percent days abstinent and time to first heavy drinking day during treatment.
can_establish: Whether, in treatment-seeking adults with alcohol dependence at US academic centres who had stopped drinking for 4 to 21 days, assignment to naltrexone, acamprosate, CBI or their combinations, each with medical management, changed self-reported drinking over 16 weeks and in the following year compared with placebo, and how a group given CBI without pills or medical management compared with placebo groups given medical management.
cannot_establish: Effects in primary care or other routine settings (the trial ran at academic sites with trained, certified and audited clinicians and up to 12 hours of research assessment), in people with psychiatric disorders requiring medication or with other drug use disorders (excluded), or beyond 1 year after treatment; whether combinations add or subtract benefit (power for interactions was estimated at 0.40 to 0.50); a placebo effect separate from fewer clinical contacts and open assignment in the no-pill group; or effects on objectively measured drinking (the biomarkers showed no differential treatment effects).

sample.recruitment: Advertisements and clinical referrals at 11 US academic sites (treatment-seeking volunteers). Of 4965 volunteers screened by telephone, 2928 were excluded at telephone screening and 654 at baseline screening; 1383 were randomized, slightly above the protocol target of 1375 (Methods › Recruitment and Randomization, 1st paragraph, p. 2004; Figure 1, p. 2005; Results › Study Population, 1st paragraph, p. 2007).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: DSM-IV alcohol dependence by the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV; 4 to 21 days of abstinence; more than 14 (women) or 21 (men) drinks a week, with at least 2 heavy drinking days (4 or more drinks a day for women, 5 or more for men) in a consecutive 30-day period within the 90 days before baseline. Excluded: DSM-IV abuse of other substances (except nicotine or cannabis) in the last 90 days (6 months for opiates) or a positive urine drug screen; a psychiatric disorder requiring medication; unstable medical conditions, for example liver enzymes above 3 times the upper limit of normal (Methods › Recruitment and Randomization, 2nd paragraph, p. 2004).
sample.demographics: 428 women and 955 men; median age 44; 71% with at least 12 years of education; 42% married; 23% (321) from ethnic minorities; in the 30 days before randomization 2.3% had been medically detoxified and 7.7% had inpatient treatment; abstinence at randomization was 4 days in 42%, 5 to 7 days in 24%, 8 to 14 in 18% and 15 to 21 in 15% (Results › Study Population, p. 2007). By group (Table 1, p. 2008): mean age 43.2 to 45.4; men 67.3% to 71.6%; current smokers 48.7% to 61.5%; in the 30 days before randomization, percent days abstinent 22.9 to 29.8, drinks per drinking day 11.8 to 13.2 and heavy drinking days 19.0 to 20.1.
sample.attrition: End of treatment (no drinking assessment at week 16; Figure 1, p. 2005): MM + placebo 9, MM + naltrexone 12, MM + acamprosate 7, MM + both 7, MM + CBI + placebo 9, MM + CBI + naltrexone 7, MM + CBI + acamprosate 7, MM + CBI + both 12, CBI only 8; 78 of 1383 in all (5.6%, editors' sum). 94% (92% to 96% by group) provided complete within-treatment drinking data (Results › Data Completeness, p. 2007). Percent days abstinent was analysed in 1376, excluding 7 without any post-randomization drinking data (2 in MM + CBI + placebo, 3 in MM + CBI + both, 2 in CBI only); time to heavy drinking used all 1383, with those lost counted as relapsed from the day after their last contact. One year after treatment (no drinking data at the final assessment; Table 6, p. 2012): MM + placebo 26 (17.0%), MM + naltrexone 28 (18.2%), MM + acamprosate 26 (17.1%), MM + both 25 (16.9%), MM + CBI + placebo 22 (14.1%), MM + CBI + naltrexone 25 (16.1%), MM + CBI + acamprosate 21 (13.9%), MM + CBI + both 32 (20.4%), CBI only 34 (21.7%); P=.68; 239 in all (17.3%, editors' sum). The text gives an average 1-year completion rate of 82.3% (range 80% to 87%), apparently on a different definition (p. 2007). Discontinuation of medication by arm is in key finding 12.
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers seeking treatment, recruited largely by advertisement at academic centres, who reached at least 4 days of abstinence, mostly as outpatients, and had no psychiatric disorder requiring medication and no other drug use disorder; 3582 of 4965 screened (72%) were excluded. The authors list the intensive research assessments (up to 12 hours), recruitment and treatment at academic rather than primary care sites, the exclusions and the 16-week treatment as limits to generalizability (Comment, 9th paragraph, p. 2015).

exposure.measurement: Randomized assignment to the interventions. Medication adherence by returned blister-pack counts (mean 85.8%, median 96.4%); MM and CBI attendance by sessions completed (medians 9 and 10); MM and CBI sessions audiotaped, with 8% and 12% monitored for protocol adherence (pp. 2006–2008).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: oral naltrexone to a target of 100 mg a day and acamprosate 3 g a day, or matching placebos, for 16 weeks, doses the authors chose above those commonly prescribed; on average 88 mg of naltrexone and 2537 mg of acamprosate were taken daily. MM: 9 sessions over 16 weeks (the first about 45 minutes, later ones about 20). CBI: up to twenty 50-minute sessions. The CBI-only group had access to a health care professional at weeks 4, 8, 12 and 16 for liver tests and advice (pp. 2006–2007).
exposure.polysubstance: People with DSM-IV abuse of other substances in the previous 90 days (6 months for opiates) or a positive urine drug screen were excluded, except for nicotine and cannabis; 48.7% to 61.5% of each group smoked (Table 1). Drug use other than alcohol during the trial is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: 4 to 21 days of abstinence were required before randomization (42% had 4 days). The outcomes are drinking during the 16 weeks of treatment and in the following year.

comparison.controls: For each medication, matching placebo pills with MM; for CBI, MM without CBI. For the separate question of pill-taking and MM, the CBI-only group (no pills, no MM) was compared with placebo + MM and with placebo + MM + CBI.
comparison.matching: Randomization (permuted blocks of 9, stratified by site); 76 baseline characteristics compared, with one nominal difference (DSM-IV dependence symptoms 5.4 vs 5.6, CBI vs no-CBI groups) (p. 2007).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not a concern in the usual sense, as assignment was random; baseline drinking, dependence severity, craving, consequences, smoking and biomarkers were measured (Table 1). Psychiatric symptoms not requiring medication are not reported by group.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same exclusions in all groups; smoking similar across groups (48.7% to 61.5%, P=.54).

outcomes.instruments: Drinking: Form 90 structured interview at baseline and a timeline followback calendar during treatment, collected by research assistants at the 9 MM visits (and at the same times in the CBI-only group) and at 2-hour assessments at weeks 8, 16, 26, 52 and 68. Craving: Obsessive Compulsive Drinking Scale (OCDS). Consequences: Drinker Inventory of Consequences (DrInC). Biomarkers: γ-glutamyltransferase (GGT) and percent carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (%CDT) at baseline and weeks 8 and 16. Adverse events: SAFTEE interview by a health care professional at each visit, with blood counts and liver and kidney tests every 4 weeks (pp. 2004–2005).
outcomes.validity_norms: Self-reported drinking was checked against %CDT at group level only: participants reporting complete abstinence (n=212) had a 15% fall in %CDT and those reporting any drinking (n=694) a 5% rise (p. 2008); no individual-level agreement is reported, and neither GGT nor %CDT showed differential treatment effects (p. 2011).
outcomes.operationalization: Percent days abstinent computed monthly over the 16 weeks (at least 5 days of data per month, otherwise missing). Heavy drinking day: 5 or more standard drinks for men, 4 or more for women. Standard drink: 0.5 oz of absolute alcohol, equivalent to 10 oz of beer, 4 oz of wine or 1.0 oz of 100-proof liquor (p. 2006); editors' conversion, taking US fluid ounces and 0.789 g/mL: about 14.8 mL or 11.7 g of ethanol. Good clinical outcome over the last 8 weeks of treatment: abstinence, or moderate drinking (at most 11 drinks a week for women and 14 for men, with no more than 2 days above 3 drinks for women or 4 for men) without problems (3 or more DrInC items) (p. 2007; Figure 4 legend, p. 2012).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni α=.025 for the two coprimary end points (97.5% CIs); within each, 3 main effects and 4 interactions were tested at .025 without further adjustment (pp. 2006–2007). Post hoc pairwise tests for the CBI-only comparisons were corrected for multiple comparisons, method not stated (p. 2011). Secondary outcomes were tested without correction. The 11 counted: percent days abstinent, time to first heavy drinking day, drinks per drinking day, drinks per day, heavy drinking days per month, time to first drink, OCDS, DrInC, GGT, %CDT and the composite clinical outcome; three of them were analysed again for the year after treatment, and adverse events were tabulated separately.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Participants and all site staff (investigators, research staff, evaluators, MM clinicians, CBI therapists) were blind to medication through treatment and the 1-year follow-up (pp. 2005–2006). The research assistants who collected drinking and craving data were not blind to psychosocial treatment (CBI or none) (p. 2004), and the CBI-only group was open by design. No check of whether participants could tell their medication is reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Percent days abstinent during treatment, least-squares means adjusted for site and baseline (Table 3, p. 2009): main effects acamprosate 78.4 vs placebo 77.6 (P=.61), naltrexone 78.8 vs 77.2 (P=.25), CBI 78.2 vs 77.8 (P=.82); naltrexone × CBI interaction P=.009, with placebo without CBI 75.1, naltrexone without CBI 80.6, CBI with placebo 79.2 and naltrexone + CBI 77.1 (pooled over acamprosate). Cohen d with 97.5% CI against placebo naltrexone without CBI (Figure 2, p. 2010): naltrexone without CBI 0.22 (0.03 to 0.40), CBI without naltrexone 0.17 (−0.02 to 0.35), both 0.07 (−0.11 to 0.25); main-effect d 0.02, 0.06 and 0.01, all intervals including 0. Time to first heavy drinking day, hazard ratios with 97.5% CI (Figure 2): naltrexone 0.72 (0.53 to 0.98; P=.02), acamprosate 0.85 (0.63 to 1.15; P=.23), CBI 0.81 (0.60 to 1.10; P=.16); naltrexone × CBI P=.15; against placebo naltrexone without CBI, naltrexone without CBI 0.78 (0.63 to 0.97), CBI without naltrexone 0.84 (0.68 to 1.05), both 0.91 (0.74 to 1.13). With at least one heavy drinking day by week 16 (Table 4, p. 2010): naltrexone 68.2% vs placebo 71.4%; acamprosate 69.6% vs 70.1%; CBI 70.0% vs 69.7%. Composite good clinical outcome, odds ratios with 95% CI against placebo naltrexone without CBI (Figure 4, p. 2012): naltrexone without CBI 2.16 (1.46 to 3.20), CBI 1.82 (1.26 to 2.65), both 1.93 (1.33 to 2.80); numbers needed to treat as printed: naltrexone 6, CBI 7, naltrexone + CBI 7 (p. 2011). Editors' calculation of absolute differences: naltrexone without CBI vs placebo, 5.5 percentage points of abstinent days (about 6 days of 112); MM + naltrexone vs MM + placebo, 7.7 percentage points fewer with a heavy drinking day (67.5% vs 75.2%, Table 5).
analysis.covariates: Baseline percent days abstinent (30 days before the last drink) and site in all models: a mixed-effects general linear model for percent days abstinent with the three treatments as fixed effects and month as a repeated measure, an analogous proportional hazards model for time to heavy drinking, and logistic models for the composite (p. 2006). Site had a significant main effect in most analyses, with no site × treatment interaction (pp. 2008–2009).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Registered at clinicaltrials.gov, NCT00006206 (abstract, p. 2003). The registration date and the registered outcomes are not given in the paper, and the registry record was not read for this card (PDF readers in this round had no browser). The paper states that the protocol, published as a design paper (ref. 22, not read), prospectively specified two intent-to-treat analyses in the 8 pill groups with the coprimary end points percent days abstinent and time to first heavy drinking day over the 16 weeks of treatment (Statistical Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 2006); these are the outcomes reported in Tables 3 and 4 and Figure 2. The CBI-only comparisons, the 1-year follow-up, alternative drinking measures and the composite outcome are described as preplanned secondary analyses (p. 2007).
analysis.selective_reporting: All prespecified main effects and interactions for both coprimary outcomes are tabulated, including the nulls. The abstract foregrounds the decomposed naltrexone × CBI interaction and the naltrexone hazard ratio; how the main-effect hazard ratios were estimated is not stated (reporting issue 1). Adverse events are not reported for the CBI-only group.
analysis.power: Power above 0.90 for a 10% main effect of each treatment on each coprimary end point (the paper does not say 10% of what), and 0.40 to 0.50 for an interaction half that size: the steering committee chose to ensure the main effects and settle for modest power for interactions (Statistical Methods, 4th paragraph, p. 2007). The trial was therefore not powered to show or exclude the interactions it reports.

interpretation_gap.results_show: During 16 weeks all groups reduced drinking substantially. Acamprosate had no effect on any outcome. Neither naltrexone nor CBI had a significant main effect on abstinent days; a naltrexone × CBI interaction (P=.009) arose because, within MM, naltrexone without CBI gave more abstinent days than placebo (80.6 vs 75.1; d 0.22, 97.5% CI 0.03 to 0.40), while CBI with placebo (79.2) and the combination (77.1) did not differ significantly from placebo. Naltrexone lowered the hazard of a first heavy drinking day (HR 0.72), an estimate that appears to come from the MM-only cells; across all pill groups 68.2% vs 71.4% had a heavy drinking day. The no-pill CBI group had fewer abstinent days than the placebo groups given MM, without significant differences in relapse or global outcome. In the year after treatment the naltrexone × CBI interaction disappeared (P=.27), the gaps between the cells did not shrink (4.8 to 5.9 points from the placebo cell, against 2.0 to 5.5 during treatment; the CBI main-effect gap widened from 0.4 to 3.1 points, P=.08), and none met the trial's significance threshold. The biomarkers showed no differential treatment effects.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that patients receiving MM with naltrexone, CBI or both "fared better on drinking outcomes", that acamprosate showed no evidence of efficacy, that no combination did better than naltrexone or CBI alone, that placebo pills and meeting a health care professional had a positive effect beyond CBI, and that naltrexone with MM could be delivered in health care settings (p. 2003); the Comment calls 0.28 the reduction in risk of a first heavy drinking day with naltrexone (1st paragraph, p. 2013). Gaps: (1) only naltrexone versus placebo without CBI was significant; the Results say the other two comparisons were trends (p. 2010), but the abstract groups CBI and the combination with naltrexone; (2) the hazard ratio of 0.72 is presented as a main effect of naltrexone, while its interval fits a comparison of two cells of about 150 people each (reporting issue 1); (3) the placebo-effect conclusion rests on abstinent days in an open, no-pill group that had access to a health professional at 4 visits (for liver tests and advice) instead of 9 MM sessions; relapse (P=.05) and global outcome (P=.07) did not differ significantly, and the difference was gone at 1 year; (4) delivery in ordinary health care settings was not tested, as the authors' own list of limits shows (p. 2015); (5) the abstract gives no absolute effects: 5.5 percentage points of abstinent days, about 6 days in 16 weeks, and 7.7 points fewer people with a heavy drinking day in the MM-only cells (editors' calculations). The Results, by contrast, report the null main effects, and the Comment states the fading of effects after treatment and the limits to generalizability plainly.

timeline.event: Veterans Affairs Naltrexone Cooperative Study (Krystal et al., 2001): a negative multisite naltrexone trial, which the authors contrast with their result and attribute to differences in participants, 12-step facilitation, a high placebo response, lower follow-up and smaller size (Comment, 1st paragraph, p. 2013; ref. 20).

Meta-analyses of naltrexone trials that used 50 mg a day with specialist care (Kranzler & Van Kirk, 2001; Streeton & Whelan, 2001; Berglund et al., 2003), with which the authors say their naltrexone result is consistent (p. 2013; refs 12, 14, 55).
Kiefer et al., single-site trial suggesting a benefit from combining naltrexone and acamprosate; COMBINE does not support the combination (Comment, 3rd paragraph, p. 2013; refs 16, 58).

Mann, Lehert & Morgan, meta-analysis of acamprosate trials, among the positive results that made the null acamprosate finding surprising to the authors, who point to the short pretreatment abstinence, outpatient recruitment and more frequent assessment in COMBINE (Comment, 2nd paragraph, p. 2013; refs 13–15, 56).
This trial; the issue carries a related item on p. 2075, which is not on file.
Rösner et al., Cochrane reviews of opioid antagonists and of acamprosate for alcohol dependence (this round, read by another reader); whether they pool COMBINE is for their cards.

Jonas et al., systematic review and meta-analysis of pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorders in outpatient settings (this round, read by another reader; updated by McPheeters et al., 2023); whether and how they include COMBINE is for their cards.

replication.where_it_stands: A large factorial trial whose naltrexone result agreed with earlier naltrexone meta-analyses and disagreed with the Veterans Affairs trial, and whose null acamprosate result disagreed with most earlier acamprosate trials, as the authors set out (p. 2013); hence the status mixed. It feeds the later meta-analyses on this round's list, so claims must not count COMBINE as support independent of pooled estimates that include it, and should check which COMBINE numbers those reviews used, given reporting issue 1.

funding.funder: National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) cooperative agreements U10AA11715, 11716, 11721, 11727, 11756, 11768, 11773, 11776, 11777, 11783, 11787, 11799 and 11773 (one number printed twice), and career scientist awards K05AA014715, K05AA00133, K02DA00326 and K23AA00329. The acamprosate, naltrexone and matching placebos were donated by Lipha Pharmaceuticals, and the study was conducted under Lipha's Investigational New Drug application for acamprosate; Lipha conducted monitoring visits to the sites but, as printed, had no role in the management, analysis and interpretation of the data or in preparing or approving the manuscript. The NIAAA collaborated in design and conduct, and NIAAA staff assisted in management, analysis and interpretation of the data and commented on drafts. The study list names Mercke AG/Lipha Pharmaceuticals Inc as Investigational New Drug sponsor, site monitor and medication supplier, and Amide Pharmaceutical Inc as a further medication supplier (p. 2016).

No other disclosures were reported.
funding.affiliations_note: Eleven US academic sites and the coordinating centre (Collaborative Studies Coordinating Center, University of North Carolina); one author (Mattson) is NIAAA staff, and one (Gastfriend) is stated to be now with Alkermes. Several authors developed interventions and instruments the trial used and evaluated: the CBI manual (Miller, ref. 41), the MM manual (Pettinati, Weiss, Miller, Donovan and others, refs 39 and 40), Form 90 (Miller, ref. 26), the OCDS (Anton and colleagues, ref. 29) and the DrInC (Miller, Tonigan and Longabaugh, ref. 52). Industry ties are recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount the results; the medication supplier made one of the two drugs tested, and that drug showed no effect.

what_would_settle_it: A pragmatic trial in primary care of naltrexone against placebo with brief medical management delivered by usual clinicians, with a biomarker of drinking alongside self-report, a check on whether participants could tell their assignment, and follow-up of at least a year; and, for the placebo question, a trial randomizing placebo pills against no pills with the same amount of clinical contact.

domains.note: Permuted blocks of 9 stratified by site, assigned through a central telephone interactive voice-response system at the coordinating centre, so allocation was concealed; 76 baseline characteristics compared, one nominally different (pp. 2004, 2007). The CBI-only group's baseline craving score in Table 1 is out of line with its printed P value (reporting issue 3); that P value and the text's statement that only one comparison differed point to a misprint rather than an imbalance, but the paper does not settle it.

For the medication comparisons, identical-looking active and placebo pills in the same number for every pill group kept participants, clinicians, therapists and evaluators blind through the 1-year follow-up, and the analysis was by intention to treat, which accommodates medication discontinuation by at least 27% to 43% of each pill arm (Figure 1): low. CBI cannot be blinded and the CBI-only group knew it had no pills; co-interventions during treatment are reported only as Alcoholics Anonymous attendance of 17% to 35% across groups, without saying which (p. 2008). No check of blinding to medication is reported, although nausea (34% vs 21%) and diarrhoea (65% vs 35%) were more frequent on the active drugs.

For the 16-week coprimary outcomes: complete within-treatment drinking data for 94% (92% to 96% by group), 78 of 1383 lost by the end of treatment (7 to 12 per arm), percent days abstinent analysed in 1376, and those lost counted as relapsed in the time-to-event analysis (pp. 2005–2007). For the 1-year results (17.3% without final data, 13.9% to 21.7% by group) and for the composite outcome, whose denominators imply about 18% missing (reporting issue 2), this domain is some concerns.

Drinking was self-reported to research assistants who were blind to medication but not to CBI (p. 2004); in the CBI and no-pill comparisons both participants and assessors knew the assignment. The %CDT check is at group level only, and neither biomarker showed differential treatment effects (pp. 2008, 2011). For the medication contrasts alone this domain would be low.

The coprimary end points and the factorial analysis were prespecified in a published design paper and the trial was registered (neither read here), and every prespecified main effect and interaction is reported, including the nulls. But the time-to-heavy-drinking main-effect hazard ratios appear to be estimated within the reference cell of a model with all interactions, while the abstinent-days main effects are averaged over the factorial (reporting issue 1), and the paper does not say which estimate was prespecified; the abstract foregrounds post hoc decompositions of the interaction.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Judged for the trial's primary comparisons during the 16 weeks of treatment. The trial is large, centrally randomized and double-blind for the medications, with high retention and an intention-to-treat analysis, so the naltrexone and acamprosate contrasts are at low risk in the first four domains; the CBI and no-pill comparisons rest on self-report by participants who knew their assignment, collected by assessors who also knew it; and the basis of the main-effect hazard ratios is unclear. The trial may be cited for the absence of an acamprosate effect at the dose it gave, for a small benefit of naltrexone over placebo within medical management on abstinent days and heavy drinking during treatment, for the absence of added benefit from combining treatments, and for the no-pill comparison as a comparison of packages of care (pills and medical management against neither), not as a pure placebo effect. It may not be cited for effects in primary care or for lasting effects after treatment.

key_findings.finding: 1383 people with DSM-IV alcohol dependence were randomized at 11 US academic sites (randomization began January 2001; follow-up ended January 2004) to nine groups: MM + placebo 153, MM + naltrexone 154, MM + acamprosate 152, MM + naltrexone + acamprosate 148, MM + CBI + placebo 156, MM + CBI + naltrexone 155, MM + CBI + acamprosate 151, MM + CBI + naltrexone + acamprosate 157, and CBI alone without pills or MM 157. Of 4965 volunteers screened by telephone, 2928 were excluded at telephone screening and 654 at baseline screening.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Overview of Study Design (p. 2004); Figure 1 (p. 2005); Results › Study Population, 1st paragraph (p. 2007)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (all text read; Figure 1 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Allocation was by permuted blocks of 9, stratified by site, through a central telephone interactive voice-response system at the coordinating centre. All naltrexone and placebo pills, and all acamprosate and placebo pills, were identical in appearance, and every pill group took the same number of pills a day. Participants and all site staff (investigators, research staff, evaluators, MM clinicians and CBI therapists) were blind to medication through treatment and the 1-year follow-up; the research assistants who assessed drinking and craving were not blind to psychosocial treatment.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Recruitment and Randomization, 2nd paragraph, and Assessment, 1st paragraph (p. 2004); Assessment, 2nd paragraph (p. 2005, continuing on p. 2006); Treatment Conditions › Medications (p. 2006)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (all text read; pp. 2004–2006 checked on the rendered pages)

key_findings.finding: Study conditions: naltrexone to a target of 100 mg a day and acamprosate 3 g a day (or matching placebos) for 16 weeks, doses chosen above those commonly prescribed; on average 88 mg of naltrexone and 2537 mg of acamprosate were taken daily. MM: 9 sessions (the first about 45 minutes, later ones about 20) by 14 physicians, 28 nurses, 1 physician assistant and 1 clinical pharmacist. CBI: up to twenty 50-minute sessions by licensed specialists with at least a master's degree, combining cognitive behavioural therapy, 12-step facilitation, motivational interviewing and support-system involvement. Medians of 10 CBI and 9 MM sessions were completed; sessions were audiotaped, with 8% (MM) and 12% (CBI) monitored.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Treatment Conditions › Medications, Medical Management, Combined Behavioral Intervention and Treatment Quality Assurance (p. 2006); Results › Medication Adherence/Dose Reductions and Adherence in Behavioral Interventions (p. 2007, continuing on p. 2008)

key_findings.finding: Coprimary end points, prespecified for the 8 pill groups: percent days abstinent and time to first heavy drinking day (5 or more standard drinks a day for men, 4 or more for women) during the 16 weeks. A standard drink was 0.5 oz of absolute alcohol (10 oz of beer, 4 oz of wine or 1.0 oz of 100-proof liquor). Each outcome was analysed with a 2×2×2 factorial model (mixed model for percent days abstinent; proportional hazards model for time to heavy drinking) adjusted for site and baseline percent days abstinent; main effects and interactions were tested at a Bonferroni-corrected P=.025 (97.5% CIs) without further adjustment. Participants lost to follow-up (6%) were assumed to have resumed heavy drinking on the day after their last contact. Power was estimated above 0.90 for a 10% main effect and 0.40 to 0.50 for an interaction half that size. Editors' conversion: 0.5 US fluid ounce of ethanol is about 14.8 mL or 11.7 g (at 0.789 g/mL).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical Methods, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 2006, continuing on p. 2007) and 4th paragraph (p. 2007)
key_findings.note: The paper does not say whether the 10% main effect in the power calculation is a relative or an absolute difference.

key_findings.finding: Participants: 428 women and 955 men, median age 44, 71% with at least 12 years of education, 42% married, 23% (321) from ethnic minorities; 2.3% had been medically detoxified and 7.7% treated as inpatients in the 30 days before randomization; abstinence at randomization was 4 days in 42%, 5 to 7 in 24%, 8 to 14 in 18% and 15 to 21 in 15%. Of 76 baseline characteristics, only DSM-IV dependence symptoms differed nominally (5.4 vs 5.6, CBI vs no-CBI groups). In Table 1, percent days abstinent before randomization was 22.9 to 29.8 by group, drinks per drinking day 11.8 to 13.2, heavy drinking days 19.0 to 20.1 and current smokers 48.7% to 61.5%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study Population, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 2007); Table 1 (p. 2008)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (all text read; Table 1 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Across the pill groups, percent days abstinent rose from 25.2 at baseline to 73.1 by the end of treatment, drinks per drinking day fell 44% (12.6 to 7.1) and drinks per week fell 80% (66 to 13); every group, including placebo, improved substantially.
key_findings.locator: Results › Within-Treatment Drinking Outcomes for Pill-Taking Groups › Time Effects

key_findings.finding: Percent days abstinent during treatment (least-squares means adjusted for site and baseline): no significant main effect of acamprosate (78.4 vs 77.6 placebo; P=.61), naltrexone (78.8 vs 77.2; P=.25) or CBI (78.2 vs 77.8; P=.82); the three-factor interaction was not significant, but the naltrexone × CBI interaction was (P=.009): placebo without CBI 75.1 (n=305), naltrexone without CBI 80.6 (n=302), CBI with placebo 79.2 (n=305), naltrexone + CBI 77.1 (n=309), each pooled over acamprosate. Only naltrexone vs placebo without CBI was significant, Cohen d 0.22 (97.5% CI 0.03 to 0.40); CBI without naltrexone d 0.17 (−0.02 to 0.35); naltrexone + CBI d 0.07 (−0.11 to 0.25). Editors' calculation: 80.6 vs 75.1 is 5.5 percentage points, about 6 more abstinent days in 112.
key_findings.locator: Results › Within-Treatment Drinking Outcomes for Pill-Taking Groups › Primary Outcomes, 2nd paragraph, and 3rd paragraph (end, p. 2010); Table 3 (p. 2009); Figure 2 (p. 2010)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (all text read; Table 3 and Figure 2 checked on the rendered pages)

key_findings.finding: Time to first heavy drinking day: hazard ratio for naltrexone 0.72 (97.5% CI 0.53 to 0.98; P=.02), acamprosate 0.85 (0.63 to 1.15; P=.23), CBI 0.81 (0.60 to 1.10; P=.16); naltrexone × CBI interaction P=.15, with the same pattern as for abstinent days. Against placebo naltrexone without CBI (pooled over acamprosate): naltrexone without CBI 0.78 (0.63 to 0.97), CBI without naltrexone 0.84 (0.68 to 1.05), naltrexone + CBI 0.91 (0.74 to 1.13). With at least one heavy drinking day during treatment: naltrexone 419 of 614 (68.2%) vs placebo 437 of 612 (71.4%); acamprosate 423 of 608 (69.6%) vs 433 of 618 (70.1%); CBI 433 of 619 (70.0%) vs 423 of 607 (69.7%); without CBI, naltrexone 200 of 302 (66.2%) vs placebo 223 of 305 (73.1%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Within-Treatment Drinking Outcomes for Pill-Taking Groups › Primary Outcomes, 3rd paragraph (p. 2009); Table 4 and Figure 2 (p. 2010)
key_findings.note: Read with reporting issue 1: the intervals of the three main-effect hazard ratios fit a comparison of one treated cell with the MM + placebo cell (about 300 people), not the whole factorial.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (all text read; Table 4 and Figure 2 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: By group at the end of treatment (percent days abstinent; participants with a return to heavy drinking): MM + placebo 73.8, 115 of 153 (75.2%); MM + naltrexone 80.0, 104 of 154 (67.5%); MM + acamprosate 75.6, 108 of 152 (71.1%); MM + both 80.5, 96 of 148 (64.9%); MM + CBI + placebo 79.8, 111 of 156 (71.2%); MM + CBI + naltrexone 75.9, 103 of 155 (66.5%); MM + CBI + acamprosate 78.2, 103 of 151 (68.2%); MM + CBI + both 77.6, 116 of 157 (73.9%); CBI only 66.6, 124 of 157 (79.0%).
key_findings.locator: Table 5
key_findings.note: The relapse denominators are the randomized group sizes in the column heads of Table 5; percent days abstinent was analysed in 1376. The footnote says all drinking measures are adjusted for baseline drinking.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (Table 5 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Secondary outcomes during treatment: drinks per drinking day (P=.03), drinks per day (P=.03) and heavy drinking days per month (P=.006) all showed a significant naltrexone × CBI interaction; time to first drink showed no significant main effect or interaction. Craving (OCDS) was lower with naltrexone than placebo (9.7, SD 7.60, vs 10.9, SD 7.64; P=.01), also without the drinking items (P=.02); alcohol-related consequences showed a trend favouring naltrexone (P=.08). There were no differential treatment effects on GGT or %CDT.
key_findings.locator: Results › Within-Treatment Drinking Outcomes for Pill-Taking Groups › Secondary Outcomes, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 2010, continuing on p. 2011)

key_findings.finding: Composite good clinical outcome over the last 8 weeks of treatment (abstinence, or moderate drinking without problems): naltrexone × CBI interaction P=.02; good outcome in 58% (MM + placebo), 74% (MM + naltrexone), 71% (MM + CBI + placebo) and 74% (MM + CBI + naltrexone). Odds ratios (95% CI) against placebo naltrexone without CBI: naltrexone without CBI 2.16 (1.46 to 3.20), CBI with placebo 1.82 (1.26 to 2.65), naltrexone + CBI 1.93 (1.33 to 2.80). Numbers needed to treat as printed: 7 for CBI, 6 for naltrexone, 7 for naltrexone + CBI. Moderate drinking meant at most 11 (women) or 14 (men) drinks a week with no more than 2 days above 3 (women) or 4 (men) drinks; problems meant 3 or more items on the consequences questionnaire.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical Methods, 6th paragraph (p. 2007); Results › Clinical Significance and Table 5 (p. 2011); Figure 4 (p. 2012)
key_findings.note: See reporting issue 2: the counts and percentages in Table 5 imply about 1137 participants with composite data, not the 1294 printed, and the printed numbers needed to treat do not follow one rounding rule (editors' calculation from the printed percentages: 7.6, 6.5 and 6.2).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (all text read; Table 5 and Figure 4 checked on the rendered pages)

key_findings.finding: Mean medication adherence (returned blister-pack counts) was 85.8% (median 96.4%): acamprosate 84.2%, naltrexone 85.4%, with CBI 85.3%, without 86.3%. Ongoing or recurrent dose reductions: placebo 7.8%, acamprosate 11.9%, naltrexone 12.1%, both 20.9% (P<.001). Figure 1 counts discontinuation of medication by arm (MM arm, then MM + CBI arm): placebo 46 of 153 and 42 of 156, acamprosate 66 of 152 and 50 of 151, naltrexone 57 of 154 and 51 of 155, both 58 of 148 and 66 of 157; discontinuation of all treatment was 35, 42, 39 and 36 (MM arms) and 22, 24, 23 and 37 (MM + CBI arms) in the same order; 46 of 157 in the CBI-only group stopped CBI. Alcoholics Anonymous attendance during treatment ranged from 17% to 35% across groups.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 (p. 2005); Results › Medication Adherence/Dose Reductions (p. 2007); Adherence in Behavioral Interventions (p. 2007, continuing on p. 2008)
key_findings.note: Figure 1 labels the first count Medication Only; whether the all-treatment counts are included in it is not stated, but the reasons listed for each arm sum close to the first count, which suggests they are.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (all text read; Figure 1 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: As a check on self-report, participants reporting complete abstinence over the study (n=212) had a 15% fall in %CDT from baseline to week 16, and those reporting any drinking (n=694) a 5% rise (P<.001); no individual-level agreement is reported.
key_findings.locator: Results › Biological Verification of Drinking

key_findings.finding: Adverse events during treatment (placebo, acamprosate, naltrexone, both; n=309, 303, 309, 305): nausea 21%, 24%, 34%, 42% (P<.001); vomiting 9%, 9%, 15%, 18%; diarrhoea 35%, 65%, 31%, 56%; decreased appetite 13%, 19%, 21%, 25%; somnolence 24%, 31%, 37%, 31%; AST or ALT above 5 times the upper limit of normal in 0, 1, 6 and 5 participants (P=.02); withdrawals because of adverse events 4, 9, 12 and 13 (P=.09). Of 70 serious adverse events during treatment, 2 were possibly related to study medication (1 naltrexone, 1 acamprosate), hospitalization for detoxification was the most common (n=38), and the one death was judged unrelated to medication.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse Events (p. 2008); Table 2 (p. 2009)
key_findings.note: The percentages in Table 2 run up to 2 points above count divided by column n (reporting issue 7); adverse events are not reported for the CBI-only group.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (all text read; Table 2 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: CBI alone (no pills, no MM) compared with placebo + MM and with placebo + MM + CBI during treatment: percent days abstinent 66.6 vs 73.8 vs 79.8 (overall P<.001; corrected post hoc pairs: placebo + MM vs placebo + MM + CBI P=.04, placebo + MM vs CBI alone P=.03, placebo + MM + CBI vs CBI alone P<.001); return to heavy drinking 79.0% vs 75.2% vs 71.2% (CBI alone vs placebo + MM + CBI, HR 0.77, printed 97.5% CI 0.60 to 1.00, P=.05; placebo + MM not significantly different from either); good global outcome 60.6% vs 58.2% vs 71.3% (P=.07).
key_findings.locator: Results › Within-Treatment Evaluation of CBI Therapy Without Pills (Placebo Effect), 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 2011, continuing on p. 2012); Relapse to Heavy Drinking and Global Clinical Outcome (p. 2012)
key_findings.note: The interval and the P value of the relapse comparison do not match (reporting issue 4).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (all text read; pp. 2011–2012 checked on the rendered pages)

key_findings.finding: In the year after treatment, percent days abstinent declined in all groups and the naltrexone × CBI interaction was no longer significant (P=.27): placebo + MM 61.4, naltrexone 66.2, CBI 66.6, naltrexone + CBI 67.3; CBI main effect 66.9 vs 63.8 (P=.08). More participants had a heavy drinking day than during treatment; only naltrexone showed nominally lower risk (HR 0.77, 97.5% CI 0.58 to 1.02; P=.04, above the trial's significance level), with 488 of 614 (79.5%) vs 495 of 612 (80.9%) having a heavy drinking day. CBI alone 86.6%, placebo + MM 84.3% and placebo + MM + CBI 80.8% had a heavy drinking day (not significant), with percent days abstinent of 60.9, 59.4 and 67.5 (P=.08); there was no significant group difference in good global outcome.
key_findings.locator: Results › Posttreatment Follow-up Outcomes (p. 2012, continuing on p. 2013); Table 7 (p. 2013); Tables 8 and 9 (p. 2014)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (all text read; Tables 7 to 9 checked on the rendered pages)
key_findings.note: Against Table 3, the gaps from the placebo cell were 4.8, 5.2 and 5.9 points after treatment and 5.5, 4.1 and 2.0 during it, and the CBI main-effect gap widened from 0.4 to 3.1 points (editors' calculation); what disappeared was the interaction. The Comment's statement that effects largely dissipated (key finding 17) overstates the fading for abstinent days; the abstract's description (differences of about the same size, no longer significant) fits Table 7. The four values are the naltrexone × CBI cells pooled over acamprosate, all with medical management.

key_findings.finding: Men had slightly more abstinent days than women (78.0, SD 29.12, vs 75.4, SD 19.44; P=.04), but sex did not significantly modify the response to any treatment, with limited power for such interactions. Site had a significant main effect in most analyses, with no site × treatment interactions.
key_findings.locator: Results › Site Effects (p. 2008, continuing on p. 2009); Sex Effects (p. 2011)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the treatment differences seen during treatment largely dissipated over the year after it, and list as limits to generalizability the intensive research assessments (up to 12 hours), recruitment and treatment at academic rather than primary care sites, exclusion of people with substantial concurrent psychiatric illness or other drug use, and the 16-week treatment. They suggest that the no-pill group's worse outcome may reflect disappointment at not receiving medication, optimism among those receiving pills, daily pill-taking as a reinforcer of motivation, regular meetings with a medical professional and the content of those visits.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 7th to 9th paragraphs
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (all text read; p. 2015 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: The authors' reading of CBI: given the naltrexone × CBI interaction, the main-effect tests for naltrexone and CBI should be interpreted with caution (Results, p. 2009); patients receiving medical management did better when they also received either CBI or naltrexone: without CBI naltrexone helped, without naltrexone CBI helped, and CBI plus naltrexone did not further improve outcomes (Comment, p. 2013). Among the placebo groups, corrected post hoc tests showed more abstinent days with placebo, medical management and CBI than with placebo and medical management (79.8 against 73.8, P=.04) (pp. 2011–2012).
key_findings.locator: Results › Within-Treatment Drinking Outcomes for Pill-Taking Groups › Primary Outcomes, 2nd paragraph (p. 2009); Results › Within-Treatment Evaluation of CBI Therapy Without Pills (Placebo Effect), 2nd paragraph (p. 2011, continuing on p. 2012); Comment, 1st paragraph (p. 2013)
key_findings.note: The claim on adding therapy to medicine rests on the main effect and the cell contrasts; this finding records the authors' caution and reading beside them.

key_findings.finding: The authors call the lack of acamprosate efficacy surprising and offer explanations: a higher daily dose than in most earlier trials (a study condition); only 4 days of abstinence before starting, achieved mainly as outpatients, whereas most positive acamprosate trials had a longer abstinence established during inpatient treatment; and earlier trials' less frequent assessment, non-standardised counselling and recruitment from clinical, mainly inpatient, settings.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Explanations offered, not tested; the doses are study conditions and are not recorded here.

reporting_issues.issue: The hazard ratios labelled main effects for time to first heavy drinking day (naltrexone 0.72, 0.53 to 0.98; acamprosate 0.85, 0.63 to 1.15; CBI 0.81, 0.60 to 1.10; Figure 2) come from a model fitting all main effects and 2- and 3-factor interactions (Table 4 footnote), and the coding of the factors is not stated. Editors' calculation: their 97.5% intervals imply standard errors of about 0.14 on the log scale, which corresponds to roughly 210 to 220 heavy-drinking events (4/SE²), about a quarter of the 856 events in the pill groups; MM + naltrexone against MM + placebo (no acamprosate, no CBI) has 219 events, MM + acamprosate against MM + placebo 223 and MM + CBI + placebo against MM + placebo 226 (Table 5); the 1-year naltrexone hazard ratio (0.77, 0.58 to 1.02) implies about 252 events against 250 in the same two MM-only cells (Table 9). The simple-effect hazard ratios pooled over acamprosate (0.78, 0.84, 0.91) imply about 430 to 450 events, matching their pooled cells, and the abstinent-days main effects have intervals that fit the whole factorial (d 0.06 for naltrexone, about 600 per group).
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline naltrexone hazard ratio of 0.72 is probably the contrast within MM without CBI or acamprosate (154 vs 153 people), not an effect averaged over the trial; averaged over all pill groups, 68.2% vs 71.4% had a heavy drinking day. Claims should cite 0.72 with this caveat, or the per-group counts in Table 5, until the coding is confirmed from the design paper or the data.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (Figure 2 and Tables 4, 5, 8 and 9 checked on the rendered pages)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 5 gives 1294 participants with data for the composite good clinical outcome. Editors' calculation: each of its nine cells reproduces exactly as a count divided by a whole-number denominator (for example 71 of 122 = 58.2%, 87 of 118 = 73.7%), these denominators sum to 1137, about 82% of 1383, and the odds ratios of Figure 4 are reproduced from the same denominators pooled over acamprosate. The numbers needed to treat printed in the text (7 for CBI, 6 for naltrexone, 7 for naltrexone + CBI) do not follow one rounding rule from the printed percentages: editors' calculation 1/(0.713−0.582) = 7.6, 1/(0.737−0.582) = 6.5, 1/(0.744−0.582) = 6.2.
reporting_issues.consequence: About 18% rather than 6% may lack composite data, so the composite results rest on those with data; Table 5 does not say whether its percentages are adjusted (its footnote says all drinking measures are). Numbers needed to treat should be quoted as printed with the editors' values beside them.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (Table 5 and Figure 4 checked on the rendered pages)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives the CBI-only group a baseline OCDS craving score of 18.9 (SD 9.98) against 24.5 to 26.3 (SDs about 7.6) in the other eight groups, with P=.47 for the comparison; editors' calculation from the printed means and SDs gives an F(8, 1374) of about 12.5, far from P=.47, and the text says only one of 76 baseline comparisons was nominally significant. The drinking-variable SDs in Table 1 are also almost identical across groups (percent days abstinent 24.68 to 24.78 in eight groups), which suggests model-based values; the table does not say how they were computed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the CBI-only value or its P value is misprinted, or that group started with less craving than the others; the paper does not allow a decision. If real, the no-pill comparison would be unbalanced on craving.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (Table 1 checked on the rendered page)

reporting_issues.issue: Two P values do not match their intervals. The CBI-alone against placebo + MM + CBI relapse comparison is printed as HR 0.77, 97.5% CI 0.60 to 1.00, P=.05, but a 97.5% interval reaching 1.00 implies P of about .02 (editors' calculation, Wald test from the interval), whereas P=.05 would fit a 95% interval; and the CBI main-effect hazard ratio of 0.81 (0.60 to 1.10) implies P of about .12 against the printed .16.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: either the interval label or the P value is misprinted; the CBI-alone relapse difference should be described as borderline.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (Figure 2 and p. 2012 checked on the rendered pages)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 8 (heavy drinking over the year after treatment), acamprosate × CBI row: the CBI with placebo-acamprosate cell is printed as 239 (76.8%). Editors' calculation: the row then sums to 974 against 983 in the other rows, and the per-group counts in Table 9 give 126 + 122 = 248 (79.7%); in the naltrexone × CBI row, 252 of 305 is 82.6%, printed 82.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the per-group counts of Table 9 for relapse in the year after treatment; the cell of Table 8 for CBI without acamprosate understates relapse by 9 people.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (Tables 8 and 9 checked on the rendered page)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4, acamprosate × naltrexone row: the placebo/placebo cell is printed as 227 (73.4%). Editors' calculation: the row then sums to 857 against 856 in the other rows, Table 5 gives 115 + 111 = 226 (73.1%), and 227 of 309 would be 73.5%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Trivial (one participant); the per-group counts of Table 5 should be used.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (Tables 4 and 5 checked on the rendered pages)

reporting_issues.issue: The adverse-event percentages in Table 2 run up to 2 points above count divided by column n, so the denominators are smaller than the printed n and are not stated (editors' calculation: for example diarrhoea with both drugs is 165 of 305 = 54.1%, printed 56%, and nausea with naltrexone 101 of 309 = 32.7%, printed 34%). The text's totals (70 serious adverse events; 38 hospitalizations for detoxification) are not broken down by group, while Table 2 lists 31 detoxification and 22 other serious events in the pill groups, and no adverse events are reported for the CBI-only group.
reporting_issues.consequence: Adverse-event rates should be quoted as the printed percentages with this caveat; they cannot be recomputed exactly.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (Table 2 checked on the rendered page)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 gives the no-CBI main-effect group as n=609, but Figure 1 and the table's own interaction cells (305 + 302) give 607 in the percent-days-abstinent analysis.
reporting_issues.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Anton_2006_COMBINE.pdf (Figure 1 and Table 3 checked on the rendered pages)

disagreements.first_pass: In the year after treatment the differences shrank and none met the trial's significance threshold.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 194, interpretation gap (agree, substantial), correction (1): 'the differences shrank' is not borne out for percent days abstinent; gaps from the placebo cell were 4.8, 5.2 and 5.9 points after treatment against 5.5, 4.1 and 2.0 during it, and the CBI main-effect gap grew from 0.4 to 3.1 points (P=.08); what disappeared was the interaction.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted as a factual correction after recomputing from Tables 3 and 7 (pp. 2009, 2013). The rating (substantial) is unchanged; the second reader's further suggestion for the 'claimed' field is an interpretive addition and goes to the senior author.

disagreements.resolution: Verified from Tables 3 and 7 and the Comment (p. 2015). Added to the note.

disagreements.resolution: Verified in the PDF text extraction at the three places. Added as a key finding.
